title: Heavy Vehicle National Law (2014)
design: Six jurisdictions adopted on 10 February 2014; WA and NT never did. Method: stacked difference-in-differences, net of the same comparison for unaffected industries in the same states.
comparison: Treated: ACT, NSW, QLD, SA, TAS, VIC. Comparison: NT, WA.
grade_reason: Passes the plan's pre-reform check and robustness variants; one or few treated states, so only large effects are detectable.
headline: Road freight business entry in the six jurisdictions that adopted the Heavy Vehicle National Law changed by −2.2 per 100 a year relative to WA and the NT, net of other industries (90% interval −5.9 to +0.9); exits by −1.5 (90% interval −3.8 to +0.8). Neither is distinguishable from zero.

category_summaries.competition: No detectable effect on entry or exit. A rise in entry of more than about 0.9 per 100 is ruled out, if road freight would otherwise have tracked WA and the NT; a fall is not.
category_summaries.productivity: Not measurable. Transport output per worker fell −26.2% relative to WA and the NT, far more than a freight law could plausibly cause; it most likely reflects the resources boom there. Shown for description only.

key_insights: The question: did one national law for heavy vehicles (February 2014) change how many road freight businesses started or closed?

The comparison: the six jurisdictions that adopted it against WA and the Northern Territory, which did not, from 2007-08 to 2017-18. Changes shared by every industry in the same states (a state's boom or slump) were removed by subtracting the same comparison for industries the reform did not touch.
What we found: no detectable change. Openings moved −2.2 per 100 businesses a year (90% interval −5.9 to +0.9) and closures −1.5 (−3.8 to +0.8).
How precise: a rise in openings of more than about 0.9 per 100 a year is ruled out; a fall cannot be ruled out.
What it means: no sign that the law drew in new freight firms. The comparison rests on WA and the NT, which rode the resources boom.

method.summary: Stacked difference-in-differences with clean comparison states, net of the same estimate for unaffected industries in the same states (a triple difference), with inference from placebo industries.

method.estimand: The average change in the treated industries' entry (or exit) rate in the adopting states over the exposed years, relative to the comparison states, beyond the change for unaffected industries in the same states (ACT, NSW, QLD, SA, TAS, VIC).
method.identification: Without the reform, the treated industries' rate in the adopting states would have moved as in the comparison states once state-wide changes shared with unaffected industries are removed (triple-difference parallel trends). Checked with the pre-reform event-study coefficients.
method.inference: No conventional standard errors (few treated states). p-value: two-sided rank of hat{β}^{net} among the P centred placebo estimates. 90% interval: hat{β}^{net} minus the 95th and 5th percentiles of the centred placebos (Conley and Taber 2011). Smallest detectable effect: 2.8 × their standard deviation.
steps: Took the treated industries (4610 Road Freight Transport) and the adopting states and dates from the register records; cohorts: NSW, VIC, QLD, SA, TAS, ACT from 2013-14 to 2017-18 against WA, NT. Comparison states are those not yet treated in each cohort's window.
Built yearly entry and exit rates from ABS Counts of Australian Businesses (registered release vintage), 2007-08 on, pooling the treated classes in each state.
Drew placebo groups of the same number of classes from outside the treated division, matched on size (44908 businesses in the treated states in 2012-13); 41 qualified.

Design stage with every treated outcome hidden: checked the feasibility rules (at least 100 treated businesses and 19 placebo groups) and the power, then committed the plan (docs/pap_high_evaluability.md).
Estimated the stacked difference-in-differences for the treated group and every placebo group, and subtracted the placebo mean.
Checked each pre-reform year against its 95% placebo band, and ran the registered robustness variants (the other ABS vintage, employing businesses only, leaving each state out, adding 2018-19).
Applied the plan's decision and grading rules, with Benjamini–Hochberg q-values across the batch.

caveats: WA and the NT are the only comparison jurisdictions, and both rode the resources cycle. Unaffected industries in the same states net out the common part of that cycle.
The pre-reform years pass the check, but the largest pre-reform gap (2010-11) is +6.9 per 100.
